findings.message: The sitemap.xml table contains multiple unfilled placeholder tokens ([SITEMAP_URL_COUNT], [SITEMAP_LOC_ASSESSMENT], [SITEMAP_HAS_LASTMOD], [SITEMAP_LASTMOD_ASSESSMENT], [SITEMAP_HAS_CHANGEFREQ], [SITEMAP_CHANGEFREQ_ASSESSMENT], [SITEMAP_HAS_PRIORITY], [SITEMAP_PRIORITY_ASSESSMENT], [SITEMAP_GRADE]) that were never substituted with real audit data. These are leaked template slots visible to the client.

Appendix B states 'We recorded every internal link found on every audited page: [N] links in total.' The placeholder '[N]' was never substituted with the actual total count from the audit data, leaking an unfilled template slot to the client.
findings.context: ## Appendix B: Link Inventory — 'We recorded every internal link found on every audited page: [N] links in total.'

findings.message: The Priority 3 recommendation to 'Address MX Stack Completeness, which sits at 50/100 (Could Be Better)' names only a score and a domain label. It does not identify which specific layers of the MX stack are missing or what concrete artefacts to add, making it copy-paste generic. The surrounding priority block is about Discovery Readiness; this sub-bullet introduces MX Stack Completeness without anchoring it to any specific missing element, header, file, or property.
findings.context: Priority 3, final bullet: 'Address MX Stack Completeness, which sits at 50/100 (Could Be Better). The discovery layer and the MX stack are interconnected; gaps in stack completeness reduce the metadata richness that machines use to confirm site identity and prioritise content.'

findings.message: The Priority 4 recommendation to 'Identify the primary content types across the audited set (service pages, team or contact pages, articles) and add the corresponding schema types' names generic page categories without specifying any schema type to add. No @type value, property name, or page URL is named in this bullet, making it applicable unchanged to any site audit. The specificity test fails: no data anchor appears in this bullet.
findings.context: Priority 4, first bullet: 'Identify the primary content types across the audited set (service pages, team or contact pages, articles) and add the corresponding schema types. When machines encounter typed entities with complete property sets, they are more likely to surface that content in structured or citation-eligible results, directly improving on the 65/100 score.'

findings.message: 'Where content pages carry a clear topic or service, add schema that captures that context explicitly. Machines correlating content against user queries rely on typed, property-rich markup rather than inferred meaning from prose; richer schema reduces the likelihood that relevant pages are overlooked.' This bullet names no @type, no property, no URL, and no audit-derived data point. It is pure domain framing that could appear unchanged in any schema audit for any site.
findings.context: Priority 4, third bullet: 'Where content pages carry a clear topic or service, add schema that captures that context explicitly…'

findings.message: American English spelling 'optimization' is used in the Next Steps table ('Full Optimization') and in prose ('Full Optimization' phase label). The report otherwise uses British/neutral forms (e.g. 'optimise' in scoring methodology). This creates a mixed-register inconsistency within the same document.
findings.context: Next Steps table: '| Full Optimization | P1, P2, P3, P4 (P1-P4) | Full machine readiness …'

findings.message: 'the picture that emerges for human visitors is a confident one' implies that the machine-experience picture is the opposite — not confident. This is inverse framing that casts the machine-readiness findings in a subtly negative light without stating a neutral score.
findings.context: Executive Summary: 'We audited eleven pages of www.dkd.de on 22 May 2026, and the picture that emerges for human visitors is a confident one.'
